questions.q: Which medallion layer corresponds to Lesson 11's 'cleansed' zone?
options: Silver
Gold
Bronze
There is no equivalent layer
questions.explain: Bronze=Raw, Silver=Cleansed, Gold=Curated — the same three jobs, different vocabulary.

questions.q: Where does the term 'medallion architecture' and the Bronze/Silver/Gold naming come from?
options: Microsoft Azure specifically
The original Hadoop project
Databricks
It has no specific origin
questions.explain: Bronze/Silver/Gold is the vocabulary you'll hear in almost every real Databricks job and piece of documentation.

questions.q: What is the one genuine difference medallion architecture typically expects, beyond just naming?
options: There is no real difference at all — it's purely vocabulary
Every layer is typically stored as a Delta table, not just Parquet files in a folder, enabling incremental updates
Medallion architecture forbids using Parquet entirely
Medallion architecture requires exactly one storage account per layer
questions.explain: Delta's transaction log lets Silver and Gold be updated incrementally rather than fully rebuilt from Bronze each time.

questions.q: Why does this course teach both Raw/Cleansed/Curated and Bronze/Silver/Gold?
options: Only Bronze/Silver/Gold is ever used in real practice
Raw/Cleansed/Curated is tool-agnostic vocabulary, while Bronze/Silver/Gold is what you'll hear in almost every real Databricks conversation — knowing both lets you follow either
They are actually unrelated patterns that happen to sound similar
Raw/Cleansed/Curated is the newer, more modern naming
questions.explain: Both namings describe the same pattern; this course deliberately teaches both so students recognize either.

questions.q: What does incremental updating via a Delta table's transaction log avoid?
options: The need for partitioning
Fully rebuilding Silver or Gold tables from Bronze every single time new data arrives
The need for RBAC or ACL permissions
The need for any Bronze layer at all
questions.explain: Merging new data in incrementally is far more efficient than a full rebuild — this is covered in depth in this track's Databricks course.
